summary: This article explains why Jupiter is called the king of the planets: its giant size, gas body and stripes, the Great Red Spot storm, its fast spin and long year, its large moons, and the spacecraft that study it.
introduce: Draw a simple cause → effect arrow on the board and ask students for an everyday example, such as “I did not sleep, so I felt tired.” Tell them that while reading “Jupiter: King of the Planets” they will find at least two cause-and-effect links.

keyTerms.def: the layer of gases around a planet
to turn around a center point, like a spinning top
a tool with lenses or mirrors that makes faraway things look bigger and closer

challengeTerms.def: the lightest and most common gas in the universe
the amount of matter, or stuff, in an object
having to do with volcanoes, which send out hot melted rock, ash, and gas

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that Jupiter is a more interesting planet to study than Earth? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Choose two features of Jupiter from the article and explain how each one is different from Earth.
struggling: Pre-teach atmosphere, rotate, and telescope with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers match cause cards to effect cards from the article with a partner.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses hydrogen, mass, and volcanic to explain one important cause-and-effect chain from the article.
